thread.title: Crazy day for stocks, Dow — expect more volatility and even some Bette Davis

author: Mike Sunnucks
title: Crazy day for stocks, Dow — expect more volatility and even some Bette Davis
text: – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Feb 6, 2018, 2:53pm MST Updated Feb 6, 2018, 7:30pm MST Stock markets had a wild ride today with the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing up 567 points after having more than 1,100-point swings. Expect more volatility as investors and markets look at a strong U.S. economy, consumer spending and corporate earnings and weigh those against concerns about budget deficits, higher interest rates and better yields on U.S. Treasury notes and bonds. “The question is which emotion is going to carry the day — greed or fear,” said Christopher Lamoureux , a finance professor and stock market expert at the University of Arizona . Lamroureux said the greed or fear dynamic explained the roller coaster day on Wall Street that saw the Dow Jones Industrial Average close at 24,912.77. That — and a 2 percent jump for the Nasdaq and 1.7 percent gain for the S&P 500 — comes after the big losses on Monday and last week. Lamoureux said he’s continuing to watch the VIX index. The VIX, CBOE Volatility Index, is a stock market volatility gauge. It closed at 29.70 today after being as high as $38 during recent drops, Lamoureux said. The University of Arizona professor said the VIX has been as low as 10 or 11 and averaging around 15. He expects to see continue volatile trading days until the VIX gets below 20. Lamoureux even reference the famous Bette Davis quote “Fasten your seatbelts. It’s going to be a bumpy night.” Despite the markets' wild fluctuations, Lamoureux said the U.S. economy continues to show strength “The economy is still going strong,” he said. Corporate earnings also continue to show strength — witnesses by gains today from Walt Disney Co. (NYSE: DIS), Snapchat parent Snap (NYSE: SNAP) and Coach and Kate Spade parent Tapestry (NYSE: TPR). There are concerns about the Trump tax cuts' impacts on budget deficits, interest rate hikes and tighter monetary policies from the Federal Reserve Bank. All that has moved up yields on bonds and U.S. Treasury notes that finance federal debt. The 10-year Treasury yield closed up and at 2.8 percent today, the 30-year was down but still at more than 3 percent, according to CNBC. That gives investors and fund managers incentives to put money there (risk-free) instead of stocks, according to Geoffrey Smith , a finance professor and stock market expert at Arizona State University . The Trump tax cuts may have trimmed rates and resulted in employee bonuses from the likes of Home Depot (NYSE: HD), Southwest Airlines (NYSE: LUV), American Airlines (Nasdaq: AAL) and Bank of America (NYSE: BAC) as well as $350 billion domestic investment program from Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL). But Smith said without spending cuts, the tax reductions magnify deficit and how to pay them off. That increases Treasury yield and could push capital away from stocks. Lamoureux said investors and markets will likely being weighing its concerns against upsides for a while. “Risk — that four letter word can matter sometimes,” he said. – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Feb 6, 2018, 2:53pm MST Updated Feb 6, 2018, 7:30pm MST Related Content
